profile.campus: Chandler, Maricopa County, Arizona (CyrusOne Phoenix-metro campus, PHX1-PHX8)
profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own facility materials and an aggregator listing dedicated to this specific building, PHX1-PHX8 sits at 2305-2335 South Ellis Street Chandler, AZ 85286, part of CyrusOne's roughly 2,000,000 sq ft, eight-building Chandler campus (PHX1 through PHX8) totaling a publicly stated 169 MW of IT capacity across the whole campus; that campus-wide MW figure is not confirmed as this individual building's own capacity, so it is not asserted here as a single-building number.

Wikipedia's entry on CyrusOne states the company acquired 55.9 acres in Chandler in September 2011 for data center construction, part of its early-2010s national expansion under then-parent Cincinnati Bell before CyrusOne's own 2013 IPO; the company was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, headquartered in Dallas, Texas, and was taken private in a roughly $15 billion deal when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) acquired it, closing in March 2022. Chandler's electric and water utility, Salt River Project (SRP), serves this part of the Phoenix metro; Arizona data centers' water-intensive cooling systems have drawn scrutiny from local outlets including the Phoenix New Times given the state's arid climate and ongoing water-supply debates, a regional context relevant to this campus though not a site-specific consumption figure confirmed for this particular building.

Chandler's broader appeal to data center operators, alongside CyrusOne, the same submarket has drawn large campuses from other hyperscale and colocation players, stems from Arizona's relatively low natural-disaster risk profile (limited seismic activity, no hurricane exposure), business-friendly tax treatment for data center equipment under state statute, and proximity to fiber routes linking Phoenix to Los Angeles and other West Coast interconnection points, factors industry trade press has repeatedly cited in explaining the Phoenix metro's growth as a secondary US data center hub behind Northern Virginia and Texas.

reading.body:
The CyrusOne Chandler campus publishes 169 MW of IT capacity across eight co-located buildings, making it the largest published data center facility in Arizona and representing 33 percent of the state's 512 MW of published capacity. The campus holds certifications for financial services compliance, healthcare data handling, federal systems hosting, and physical security standards. Technical space totals 2 million square feet.

At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 169 MW of IT load translates to approximately 4,200 racks. At 8 accelerators per rack, a common configuration for GPU-based training clusters, this implies potential headroom for roughly 33,600 accelerators, though the operator publishes neither the rack count nor the customer mix, and actual AI utilization depends on tenant configuration. The campus certifications qualify it for regulated finance and healthcare workloads but do not indicate whether current tenants are AI operators.

Arizona ranks fifth nationally in published data center capacity, with 56 mapped facilities statewide but only four with published power figures. Chandler sits in the Phoenix metropolitan area, which has become a secondary hub for U.S. data center investment after the Bay Area and Northern Virginia. Whether this campus will matter to AI scaling depends on whether its tenant roster shifts toward training operations and whether grid and cooling constraints in Arizona's high-heat climate permit sustained utilization at full capacity, neither of which is published.
